Structure and functionality of cassava starch in different deep eutectic solvents/water mixtures: A comparative study
Lingyu Zengᵃ, Wei Maoᵃ, Jiawen Haoᵃ, Guirong Yeᵃ, Xueping Songᵃ, Ling Zengᵇ, Shuangfei Wangᵃ, Jinghong Zhouᵃ,*

a Guangxi Key Laboratory of Clean Pulp & Papermaking and Pollution Control, Light Industry and Food Engineering College, Guangxi University, Nanning 530004, China b Nanning Ketian Water borne Technology Co., Ltd, Nanning 530007, China
ARTICLE INFO --- *Keywords:* Deep eutectic solvents Starch Dissolution Water content

ABSTRACT Starch, as one of the most abundant natural polysaccharides, is regarded as a sustainable material due to its renewability, biodegradability, and modifiability, and is widely used as an excellent industrial material. However, as a polyhydroxyl polymer, native starch has low solubility in most situations due to its network structure formed by intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which limits its industrial application. In this study, the solubility of cassava starch (CS) in a series of acidic, neutral, and alkaline deep eutectic solvents (DESs) was investigated. Relatively high solubilities of 52.8 wt%, 11.4 wt%, and 10.2 wt% were obtained in choline chloride/formic acid (CF), ethylammonium chloride/ethylene glycol (EE), and choline chloride/diethanolamine (CD), respectively. The dissolution behavior of CS in pure mixtures of these DESs and in DESs/water mixtures (2:8) was also compared. The results of gel permeation chromatography (GPC) analysis showed that the weight-average molecular weights (Mw) and number-average molecular weights (Mn) were ranked in the order CF > EE > CD. The same pattern was observed for the DESs/water mixtures (2:8), although the reduction in Mw and Mn was less distinct than in the pure DESs. The results of X-ray diffraction, small-angle X-ray scattering, and scanning electron microscope observations were consistent with the GPC data, i.e., the hydrolysis ability of CS was higher in the acidic DESs (CF) compared to the neutral (EE) and alkaline (CD) DESs. The dissolution behaviors of CS in the DESs/water mixtures were affected by the structure of the DESs and their water content. These results demonstrate that aqueous DESs serve as excellent media for starch dissolution. Moreover, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the solubilization behavior of CS in different aqueous DESs and provides insights into the development of novel starch-based materials using DESs.

## 1. Introduction Second only to cellulose, starch is the most renewable raw material in nature; it is a natural polymer that is widely available, biocompatible, and inexpensive (Santander-Ortega et al., 2010). Native starch is a semi-crystalline polymer mainly composed of two types of α-glucan, linear amylose, and highly branched amylopectin (Fan, 2015; Lan et al., 2016; Li and Wei, 2020). It has multiple hydroxyl groups and forms intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds (Huber and Bemiller, 2000), thus creating complex hydrogen-bonded network structures, and regular

and orderly crystalline structures among polysaccharide chains of starch. These structures lead to low starch solubility in many conven- tional organic solvents (Radosta et al., 2001), which limits starch modification and its industrial application. Indeed, although starch dissolves in several solvents, such as dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Jackson, 1991; Schmitz et al., 2009), dimethylacetamide/LiCl (Heinze et al., 2000; Huang and Yu, 2010; Koganti et al., 2011), ionic liquids (Koganti et al., 2011), KOH, and NaOH (Han and Lim, 2004), high temperatures or other special conditions are typically required. DESs are a new class of ionic liquid (IL) analogs consisting of hydrogen bond acceptors and hydrogen bond donors (Abbott et al., 2007). These not only possess similar reaction properties as ILs but have the advantages of low cost, high atomic utilization, simple preparation requirements, and non-volatility (Smith et al., 2014). As such, DESs have been identified as potential alternative green solvents for polysaccharides including starches (Ren et al., 2020, 2019b; Zhang et al., 2017), cellulose (Dadi et al., 2010), lignin (Soares et al., 2017), and even biomass (Chen and Mu, 2019). Biswas et al. (2006) showed that the most complete starch dissolution was achieved in a mixture of choline chloride and urea (solubility: 9.1 wt%), and choline chloride and citric acid (solubility: 8.3 wt%) after heating at 100 °C, and the use of 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride achieved solubility of up to 15 wt% at 80 °C. Similar results were obtained for potato starch added to choline chloride/urea, choline chloride/citric acid, and choline chloride/succinic acid solutions for 60 min at temperatures ranging 118–135 °C (Zdanowicz and Spychaj, 2011). More recently, the effects of water on ILs, such as polarity, viscosity, and solvating ability, have been examined (Kohno and Ohno, 2012; Zhao et al., 2015). It has also been shown that the presence of water promotes the formation of hydrogen bonds between Ac⁻ and starch hydroxyls; a 0.15:1 mol/mol [C2mim][OAc]:water mixture effectively dissolved starch under ambient conditions without derivatization or degradation of the starch (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017). Furthermore, Lu et al. (2020) found that the IL/H2O ratio strongly influenced the appearance and microstructure of maize starch and potato starch, and water/IL mixtures offer better dissolution ability for starch than pure ILs.

Despite this existing work, few studies have considered a compre- hensive comparative analysis of starch dissolution in acidic, neutral, and alkaline aqueous DESs. Inspired by this, in this study, after screening 11 kinds of DESs composed of different hydrogen bond receptors and hydrogen bond donors for starch dissolution, we selected the following

three DESs with the highest starch dissolution rates and investigated the dissolution behavior of cassava starch (CS): (1) choline chloride/formic acid (CF), (2) ethylammonium chloride/ethylene glycol (EE), and (3) choline chloride/diethanolamine (CD). The effect of different DESs/ water ratios on the dissolution behavior of CS was also examined based on an analysis of structural changes in the starch after dissolution. Specifically, the properties and mechanisms of dissolution were studied using polarized light microscopy, scanning electron microscope (SEM) observations, X-ray diffraction (XRD), small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), attenuated total reflection-Fourier transform infrared (ATR- FTIR) spectroscopy, and gel permeation chromatography (GPC). In doing so, we provide a more comprehensive understanding of the dissolution behavior of CS in different aqueous DESs than has been previously available.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Cassava starch (0.2% moisture) was obtained from the Hongfeng Starch Co., Ltd. (Guangxi, China); choline chloride (AR, 98%), ethylamine hydrochloride (AR, 98%), and ethylene glycol (AR, 98%) were purchased from the Aladdin Industrial Co., Ltd., China; formic acid (AR, 88%) was purchased from the FUYU Fine Chemical Co., Ltd., Tianjin, China; and diethanolamine (AR, 99%) was purchased from the Damao Chemical Reagent Factory (Tianjin, China). Deionized water was used in all the experiments.

## 2.4. Starch treatment in DES/water mixtures Mixtures of the three DESs and water with different mass ratios (2:8, 4:6, 5:5, 6:4, 8:2, and 10:0) were prepared, referred to as CFW, EEW, and CDW, respectively, and where DESs/water-10:0 refers to pure DESs with no water added. Native CS (5 wt%) was added to the DESs/water mixtures and then placed in a capped 50-mL conical flask in an oil bath for 2 h at 25 °C, 60 °C, 80 °C, and 100 °C with magnetic stirring. Subsequently, ten volumes of ethanol were added with stirring. The mixtures were centrifuged at 4500 rpm for 15 min and the precipitated starch was washed three times with ethanol to remove the residual DESs. Then, for each sample, the liquid was decanted and the separated solid placed in a vacuum desiccator at 45 °C for 24 h. ## 2.6. Characterization The viscosities of the starch samples were measured using a rotational viscometer (Weiling Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd, shanghai, China) in a steady state at 22–23 °C. A transflective polarizing microscope (LEICA DM1000, Germany) and an SEM (F16502, PHENOM, Netherlands, 5 kV) were used to image the structure of the native CS and CS samples treated with the DES/water mixtures. The crystallinity of the starch samples was examined using an X-ray diffractometer (Ultima IV, RIGAKU) operating at 40 kV and 40 mA; the diffraction angle (2θ) ranged from 5° to 60°. To determine the structural characteristics of the alternating crystalline and amorphous lamellae, small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) measurements were performed with a SAXSess mc² (Antonpa, Austria) operating at 40 kV and 30 mA (λ = 0.154 nm). The chemical structures of the starch grains were determined using a Bruker TENSOR II FT-IR spectrophotometer. Spectra were recorded from 4000–400 cm⁻¹ using 32 scans and a resolution of 4 cm⁻¹. The average molecular weight and molecular weight distribution were analyzed using Agilent PL-GPC50 and Agilent PL-GPC220 GPC. Polystyrene standards were used for calibration. All measurements were performed in DMSO containing 30 mmol/L lithium bromide as the solvent.

The CS samples treated with the DES/water mixtures were used for polarizing microscope, SAXS, and GPC analyses; and the regenerated CS was used for SEM, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and attenuated total reflection-Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) analyses.

### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Solubility of starch in DESs In a series of screening experiments, a total of 11 kinds of DESs were synthesized from different hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) and hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) with different molar ratios of HBA/HBD. During the screening, the solubility of CS and viscosity were determined in in the different kinds of DESs (Table 1). We found that the acidic DESs typically achieved a higher solubility compared to the neutral and alkaline DESs (Table 1). Notably, solubility in the acidic DESs was not significantly affected by the molar ratios of HBA/HBD, and the highest starch solubility (52.8 wt%) was obtained with a CF molar ratio of 1:4. The lowest DES viscosity (10.85 mPa.s) was also obtained in the CF systems. The maximum starch solubility in the neutral and alkaline DESs was 11.4 wt% (EE 1:2) and 10.2 wt% (CD 1:8), respectively.

Several studies have reported that chloride anions play an important role in sugar solubility in ChCl-containing DESs (Hkkinen and Abbott, 2019; Zdanowicz and Spychaj, 2011). 3.2. Viscosity of the DESs/water systems Viscosity is one of the most influential factors affecting the solubility of starch, and hydrogen bonding is an important factor affecting the change in viscosity; therefore, the binding ability of hydrogen bonding is crucial. The electrostatic force, van der Waals forces, and hydrogen bond forces among the molecules are the main factors affecting the viscosity of the solvents. Fig. 1 shows the viscosities of the pure DESs (CFW-10:0, EEW-10:0, and CDW-10:0) were highest, with values of 10.85, 38.6, and 136 MPa·s, respectively. The viscosity of CDW decreased significantly with increasing water content, dropping substantially from 136 to 10.6 MPa·s when the CDW ratio was changed from 10:0–2:8. However, no distinct viscosity changes were observed for the EEW and CFW mixtures. The viscosity of pure EE was four-times greater than that of the 2:8 EEW mixture. The viscosities of the CFW-10:0 (pure CF) and CFW-2:8 mixtures were 10.85 and 2.1 MPa·s, respectively. At the same DESs/water ratio, viscosity was ranked in the order CDW > EEW > CFW.

ChCl can accept three H$^{+}$ ions; therefore, three hydrogen bonds can be formed between ChCl and diethanolamine in CD, and three hydrogen bonds can be formed between ChCl and formic acid in CF. The strong interaction between the ions in the DESs leads to high viscosity, which affects the mass transfer and contact of the two phases in the subsequent reaction process (Garcia et al., 2015).

The high viscosity of CDW-10:0 (pure CD) is explained by the strong interaction between the ions and the long molecular chain of diethanolamine. As depicted in Fig. 1, when H2O is added to pure CD, the amino or hydroxyl groups of diethanolamine can form additional hydrogen bonds with water, which leads to a decrease in the viscosity of the solvent. During the extraction of polyphenols and furanocoumarins from fig (Ficus carica L.) leaves using DESs, the extraction rates of five target compounds, including caffeoylmalic acid, were greatly improved when water was added, probably due to the reduction in viscosity and improved mass transfer (Wang et al., 2017). The lower the viscosity of the DESs, the more efficient the mass transfer between the solute and solvent becomes. Thus, a lower viscosity can improve the permeability of the DESs to CS and accelerate dissolution; water is usually used to dilute and reduce viscosity (Ren et al., 2019a, 2019b; Zhao et al., 2015).

The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic method was used to estimate the chemical properties of the DESs (Table 2). The Kamlet-Taft parameters α, β, and π* represent the hydrogen bond acidity, hydrogen bond alkalinity, and dipolarity/polarizability of a solvent, respectively (Xia et al., 2018; Xue et al., 2016). As showed in Table 2, the π* and α values of the pure DESs decreased and the β values increased with increasing pH, and pure CF had the highest α values, with similar reported by Oh et al. (2020), the α values of ChCl:FA (1:2) were greater than those of ChCl:EG (1:2). Acidic HBDs can effectively break the α-1,4 glycosidic bond between starches. In aqueous DESs, the acidity of hydrogen bonds did not change significantly, although the π* values increased due to the presence of water. The largest π* (1.34) was obtained in CDW-2:8. Compared with the pure DESs, β values were also decreased significantly in the aqueous DESs, which is explained by the fact that Cl⁻ is mostly sequestered by anionic hydrogen bonds (Ma et al., 2019).

Under polarized light, "Maltese cross" patterns are formed. ## 3.4. XRD and SAXS XRD is a useful tool for investigating the influence of DESs on the crystallinity structure of starch (Lopez-Rubio et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019). Fig. 4 shows the XRD patterns of native CS and the regenerated samples in the pure DESs and different DES/water mixtures (2:8). The native CS shows characteristic peaks typical of A-type diffraction patterns, with distinct diffraction peaks at 15°, 17°, 18°, and 23° (2θ), which is consistent with previous reports (Kim and Huber, 2008; Monroy et al., 2018). After treatment with CFW-2:8 and CFW-10:0, these diffraction peaks became flatter, indicating a much more amorphous structure. The changes in the XRD patterns of the samples treated with the EEW-2:8, EEW-10:0, CDW-2:8, and CDW-10:0 solvents were also similar; however, the diffraction peak intensities of the CFW-treated samples were flatter than those of the other treatments. This may reflect the fact that acidic CFW is more conducive to the amorphization of starch (Wang and Copeland, 2015). Furthermore, Ren et al. (2019a) reported that the main diffraction peaks of maize starch crystallites treated with water/[-C2mim][Cl]¯ and water/[C2mim][HCOO]¯ mixtures were gradually reduced; they became weaker and then disappeared owing to dissolution in association with [HCOO]¯ and [Cl]¯. Overall, the CS samples showed low and broad dispersion peaks for both pH changes and moisture content changes, which implies that the crystallinity of native starch was partially damaged or even destroyed during the dissolution process. The changes in the crystalline structure of the treated CS were also consistent with the described morphological changes.

The molecular weight distributions of the native and DESs-treated samples were determined by GPC (Table 3). The weight-average molecular weight (M_w) of the native CS was 89,179 g/mol, and the M_w to number-average molecular weight (M_n) ratio was 9.75. After treatment with different DESs/water mixtures, the molecular weight distribution decreased sharply, indicating the cleavage of glycosidic bonds. The M_w of the pure DESs (CFW-10:0, EEW-10:0, and CDW-10:0) was 231, 745, and 1066 g/mol, respectively. The molecular weight of the CDW-treated samples was higher than that of the CF and EE DESs-treated samples, which indicates that the glycosidic bonds were more stable under alkaline conditions. This is in agreement with the previously described results of the dissolution tests. M_w increased significantly with increasing water content in the DES mixtures; the M_w of CFW, EEW, and CDW was 2290, 1896, and 2811 g/mol, respectively, when the DESs/water ratio was changed from 10:0–2:8. When DESs was added with the corresponding proportion of water, the molecular weight of CS dissolved by the aqueous DESs was larger than that dissolved by the pure DESs. The presence of a moderate amount of water can reduce the by-products of the further polymerization of glucose, dehydration, etc., thus inhibiting the formation of humins and improving the glucose yield (Binder and Raines, 2010). Furthermore, this plays a regulatory role in starch modification processing by controlling moisture content.

The M_w/M_n ratio is the polydispersity coefficient, which reflects the narrow distribution of the molecules. The M_n and M_w distribution of CS can be used to characterize its solubilization by different DESs/water mixtures (Torres et al., 2020). Here, the M_w/M_n ratio of the native starch was 9.75; the lowest value (1.67) was obtained for the CFW-10:0 (pure

CF) treatment sample. This indicates that the pure CF-treated sample had the lowest polydispersion and the most uniform molecular mass distribution. The amylose content of CS ranges from 15.2% to 26.5% (Fan, 2015), which indicates that amylopectin is the main component. Compared with high-amylose starch, starch with a low amylose content is more susceptible to acid hydrolysis. Therefore, CS is considered highly susceptible to acid hydrolysis, during which the glycosidic bonds of amylose and amylopectin molecules break (Gérard et al., 2002), resulting in a rapid decline in M_w and M_n.

3.7. Starch retrogradation Starch retrogradation refers to the transformation from a disordered state to an ordered crystalline state, which for starch is often affected by the molecular structure, temperature, and other conditions (He et al., 2014). However, retrogradation often leads to changes in the hardness, viscosity, and mechanical properties of starch, as has been systematically analyzed in numerous studies (Han and Lim, 2004; Jayakody and Hoover, 2002; Karim et al., 2000). Therefore, the regeneration of CS after treatment with different DESs was also explored as part of this study.

Fig. 7 shows that the six prepared DESs were clear liquids, as has been reported elsewhere (Farooq et al., 2020); however, the mixtures became turbid after CS was added. As the temperature was increased to 100 °C, discoloration was observed for the CFW-10:0 (pure CF) mixture, whereas the CFW-2:8 mixture remained a clear, colorless liquid (Fig. 7). This indicates that the acidity of pure CF may lead to side reactions. Similar browning effects have been reported for IL-dissolved carbohydrates (Hkkinen and Abbott, 2019).

3.8. DESs/water mixture recycling and reuse To make the DESs/water mixing process more practical for industrial application, recovery and recycling capacity must be considered. Thus, recyclability of the DESs was investigated based on the reuse of the mixtures. ## 4. Conclusions The solubility of CS was explored in a series of acidic, neutral, and alkaline DESs. Three typical DESs (CF, EE, and CD) were selected and used to determine the effects of water content on their ability to dissolve CS. Based on our results, a high water content corresponded to low viscosity, and a high temperature corresponded to strong dissolvability. All three types of DESs were found to dissolve CS to varying degrees, and optimal solubility was obtained when a certain amount of water was included in the mixtures. Among the three tested DESs, the ChCl/formic acid mixture achieved the best dissolution effect, and the starch was not retrograded. Based on our findings, the composition of DESs and the water content should be considered in the process of dissolving starch, as these are crucial factors affecting subsequent mass transfer and regeneration. Overall, these findings provide valuable information to support the development of sustainable and inexpensive solvents, expanding the potential industrial application of DESs for starch, such as the conversion of reducing sugars and hydroxymethylfurfural, as well as the development of starch-based conductive materials.

However, as a polyhydroxyl polymer, native starch has low solubility in most situations due to its network structure formed by intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which limits its industrial application. In this study, the solubility of cassava starch (CS) in a series of acidic, neutral, and alkaline deep eutectic solvents (DESs) was investigated. Relatively high solubilities of 52.8 wt%, 11.4 wt%, and 10.2 wt% were obtained in choline chloride/formic acid (CF), ethylammonium chloride/ethylene glycol (EE), and choline chloride/diethanolamine (CD), respectively. The dissolution behavior of CS in pure mixtures of these DESs and in DESs/water mixtures (2:8) was also compared. The results of gel permeation chromatography (GPC) analysis showed that the weight-average molecular weights (Mw) and number-average molecular weights (Mn) were ranked in the order CF > EE > CD. The same pattern was observed for the DESs/water mixtures (2:8), although the reduction in Mw and Mn was less distinct than in the pure DESs. The results of X-ray diffraction, small-angle X-ray scattering, and scanning electron microscope observations were consistent with the GPC data, i.e., the hydrolysis ability of CS was higher in the acidic DESs (CF) compared to the neutral (EE) and alkaline (CD) DESs. The dissolution behaviors of CS in the DESs/water mixtures were affected by the structure of the DESs and their water content. These results demonstrate that aqueous DESs serve as excellent media for starch dissolution. Moreover, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the solubilization behavior of CS in different aqueous DESs and provides insights into the development of novel starch-based materials using DESs. ## 1. Introduction Second only to cellulose, starch is the most renewable raw material in nature; it is a natural polymer that is widely available, biocompatible, and inexpensive (Santander-Ortega et al., 2010). Native starch is a semi-crystalline polymer mainly composed of two types of α-glucan, linear amylose, and highly branched amylopectin (Fan, 2015; Lan et al., 2016; Li and Wei, 2020). It has multiple hydroxyl groups and forms intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds (Huber and Bemiller, 2000), thus creating complex hydrogen-bonded network structures, and regular and orderly crystalline structures among polysaccharide chains of starch. These structures lead to low starch solubility in many conven- tional organic solvents (Radosta et al., 2001), which limits starch modification and its industrial application. Indeed, although starch dissolves in several solvents, such as dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Jackson, 1991; Schmitz et al., 2009), dimethylacetamide/LiCl (Heinze et al., 2000; Huang and Yu, 2010; Koganti et al., 2011), ionic liquids (Koganti et al., 2011), KOH, and NaOH (Han and Lim, 2004), high temperatures or other special conditions are typically required. DESs are a new class of ionic liquid (IL) analogs consisting of hydrogen bond acceptors and hydrogen bond donors (Abbott et al., 2007). These not only possess similar reaction properties as ILs but have the advantages of low cost, high atomic utilization, simple preparation requirements, and non-volatility (Smith et al., 2014). As such, DESs have been identified as potential alternative green solvents for polysaccharides including starches (Ren et al., 2020, 2019b; Zhang et al., 2017), cellulose (Dadi et al., 2010), lignin (Soares et al., 2017), and even biomass (Chen and Mu, 2019). Biswas et al. (2006) showed that the most complete starch dissolution was achieved in a mixture of choline chloride and urea (solubility: 9.1 wt%), and choline chloride and citric acid (solubility: 8.3 wt%) after heating at 100 °C, and the use of 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride achieved solubility of up to 15 wt% at 80 °C. Similar results were obtained for potato starch added to choline chloride/urea, choline chloride/citric acid, and choline chloride/succinic acid solutions for 60 min at temperatures ranging 118–135 °C (Zdanowicz and Spychaj, 2011). More recently, the effects of water on ILs, such as polarity, viscosity, and solvating ability, have been examined (Kohno and Ohno, 2012; Zhao et al., 2015). It has also been shown that the presence of water promotes the formation of hydrogen bonds between Ac⁻ and starch hydroxyls; a 0.15:1 mol/mol [C2mim][OAc]:water mixture effectively dissolved starch under ambient conditions without derivatization or degradation of the starch (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017). Furthermore, Lu et al. (2020) found that the IL/H2O ratio strongly influenced the appearance and microstructure of maize starch and potato starch, and water/IL mixtures offer better dissolution ability for starch than pure ILs. Despite this existing work, few studies have considered a compre- hensive comparative analysis of starch dissolution in acidic, neutral, and alkaline aqueous DESs. Inspired by this, in this study, after screening 11 kinds of DESs composed of different hydrogen bond receptors and hydrogen bond donors for starch dissolution, we selected the following three DESs with the highest starch dissolution rates and investigated the dissolution behavior of cassava starch (CS): (1) choline chloride/formic acid (CF), (2) ethylammonium chloride/ethylene glycol (EE), and (3) choline chloride/diethanolamine (CD). The effect of different DESs/ water ratios on the dissolution behavior of CS was also examined based on an analysis of structural changes in the starch after dissolution. Specifically, the properties and mechanisms of dissolution were studied using polarized light microscopy, scanning electron microscope (SEM) observations, X-ray diffraction (XRD), small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), attenuated total reflection-Fourier transform infrared (ATR- FTIR) spectroscopy, and gel permeation chromatography (GPC). In doing so, we provide a more comprehensive understanding of the dissolution behavior of CS in different aqueous DESs than has been previously available. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Cassava starch (0.2% moisture) was obtained from the Hongfeng Starch Co., Ltd. Three typical DESs (CF, EE, and CD) were selected and used to determine the effects of water content on their ability to dissolve CS. Based on our results, a high water content corresponded to low viscosity, and a high temperature corresponded to strong dissolvability. All three types of DESs were found to dissolve CS to varying degrees, and optimal solubility was obtained when a certain amount of water was included in the mixtures. Among the three tested DESs, the ChCl/formic acid mixture achieved the best dissolution effect, and the starch was not retrograded. Based on our findings, the composition of DESs and the water content should be considered in the process of dissolving starch, as these are crucial factors affecting subsequent mass transfer and regeneration. Overall, these findings provide valuable information to support the development of sustainable and inexpensive solvents, expanding the potential industrial application of DESs for starch, such as the conversion of reducing sugars and hydroxymethylfurfural, as well as the development of starch-based conductive materials. In this study, the solubility of cassava starch (CS) in a series of acidic, neutral, and alkaline deep eutectic solvents (DESs) was investigated. The results of gel permeation chromatography (GPC) analysis showed that the weight-average molecular weights (Mw) and number-average molecular weights (Mn) were ranked in the order CF > EE > CD. The same pattern was observed for the DESs/water mixtures (2:8), although the reduction in Mw and Mn was less distinct than in the pure DESs. The results of X-ray diffraction, small-angle X-ray scattering, and scanning electron microscope observations were consistent with the GPC data, i.e., the hydrolysis ability of CS was higher in the acidic DESs (CF) compared to the neutral (EE) and alkaline (CD) DESs. The dissolution behaviors of CS in the DESs/water mixtures were affected by the structure of the DESs and their water content. These results demonstrate that aqueous DESs serve as excellent media for starch dissolution. Introduction Second only to cellulose, starch is the most renewable raw material in nature; it is a natural polymer that is widely available, biocompatible, and inexpensive (Santander-Ortega et al., 2010). Native starch is a semi-crystalline polymer mainly composed of two types of α-glucan, linear amylose, and highly branched amylopectin (Fan, 2015; Lan et al., 2016; Li and Wei, 2020). It has multiple hydroxyl groups and forms intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonds (Huber and Bemiller, 2000), thus creating complex hydrogen-bonded network structures, and regular and orderly crystalline structures among polysaccharide chains of starch. These structures lead to low starch solubility in many conven- tional organic solvents (Radosta et al., 2001), which limits starch modification and its industrial application. Indeed, although starch dissolves in several solvents, such as dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (Jackson, 1991; Schmitz et al., 2009), dimethylacetamide/LiCl (Heinze et al., 2000; Huang and Yu, 2010; Koganti et al., 2011), ionic liquids (Koganti et al., 2011), KOH, and NaOH (Han and Lim, 2004), high temperatures or other special conditions are typically required. Similar results were obtained for potato starch added to choline chloride/urea, choline chloride/citric acid, and choline chloride/succinic acid solutions for 60 min at temperatures ranging 118–135 °C (Zdanowicz and Spychaj, 2011). More recently, the effects of water on ILs, such as polarity, viscosity, and solvating ability, have been examined (Kohno and Ohno, 2012; Zhao et al., 2015). It has also been shown that the presence of water promotes the formation of hydrogen bonds between Ac⁻ and starch hydroxyls; a 0.15:1 mol/mol [C2mim][OAc]:water mixture effectively dissolved starch under ambient conditions without derivatization or degradation of the starch (Zhang et al., 2015, 2017). Furthermore, Lu et al. (2020) found that the IL/H2O ratio strongly influenced the appearance and microstructure of maize starch and potato starch, and water/IL mixtures offer better dissolution ability for starch than pure ILs. Despite this existing work, few studies have considered a compre- hensive comparative analysis of starch dissolution in acidic, neutral, and alkaline aqueous DESs. Inspired by this, in this study, after screening 11 kinds of DESs composed of different hydrogen bond receptors and hydrogen bond donors for starch dissolution, we selected the following three DESs with the highest starch dissolution rates and investigated the dissolution behavior of cassava starch (CS): (1) choline chloride/formic acid (CF), (2) ethylammonium chloride/ethylene glycol (EE), and (3) choline chloride/diethanolamine (CD). The effect of different DESs/ water ratios on the dissolution behavior of CS was also examined based on an analysis of structural changes in the starch after dissolution. Specifically, the properties and mechanisms of dissolution were studied using polarized light microscopy, scanning electron microscope (SEM) observations, X-ray diffraction (XRD), small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), attenuated total reflection-Fourier transform infrared (ATR- FTIR) spectroscopy, and gel permeation chromatography (GPC). In doing so, we provide a more comprehensive understanding of the dissolution behavior of CS in different aqueous DESs than has been previously available. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. The presence of a moderate amount of water can reduce the by-products of the further polymerization of glucose, dehydration, etc., thus inhibiting the formation of humins and improving the glucose yield (Binder and Raines, 2010). The M_w/M_n ratio is the polydispersity coefficient, which reflects the narrow distribution of the molecules. The M_n and M_w distribution of CS can be used to characterize its solubilization by different DESs/water mixtures (Torres et al., 2020). Here, the M_w/M_n ratio of the native starch was 9.75; the lowest value (1.67) was obtained for the CFW-10:0 (pure CF) treatment sample. This indicates that the pure CF-treated sample had the lowest polydispersion and the most uniform molecular mass distribution. The amylose content of CS ranges from 15.2% to 26.5% (Fan, 2015), which indicates that amylopectin is the main component. Compared with high-amylose starch, starch with a low amylose content is more susceptible to acid hydrolysis. Therefore, CS is considered highly susceptible to acid hydrolysis, during which the glycosidic bonds of amylose and amylopectin molecules break (Gérard et al., 2002), resulting in a rapid decline in M_w and M_n. 3.7. DESs/water mixture recycling and reuse To make the DESs/water mixing process more practical for industrial application, recovery and recycling capacity must be considered. Thus, recyclability of the DESs was investigated based on the reuse of the mixtures. As shown in Fig. 8, the recovered DESs maintained good CS solubility (approximately 80%) after being reused three times. However, CDW-10:0 showed poor reusability due to its excessive viscosity. ## 4. Conclusions The solubility of CS was explored in a series of acidic, neutral, and alkaline DESs. Three typical DESs (CF, EE, and CD) were selected and used to determine the effects of water content on their ability to dissolve CS. Based on our results, a high water content corresponded to low viscosity, and a high temperature corresponded to strong dissolvability. All three types of DESs were found to dissolve CS to varying degrees, and optimal solubility was obtained when a certain amount of water was included in the mixtures. Among the three tested DESs, the ChCl/formic acid mixture achieved the best dissolution effect, and the starch was not retrograded. Based on our findings, the composition of DESs and the water content should be considered in the process of dissolving starch, as these are crucial factors affecting subsequent mass transfer and regeneration. Overall, these findings provide valuable information to support the development of sustainable and inexpensive solvents, expanding the potential industrial application of DESs for starch, such as the conversion of reducing sugars and hydroxymethylfurfural, as well as the development of starch-based conductive materials.
